title: Electrifying the NH-66 corridor in Keralam for battery electric trucks - International Council on Clean Transportation
source_name: 国际清洁交通委员会 ICCT
content: Charging infrastructure needed to support India’s full transition to battery electric trucks by 2050 Report Electrifying the NH-66 corridor in Keralam for battery electric trucks Keralam has set out to build India’s first state-led electric truck corridor along National Highway 66 (NH-66). The corridor runs over 622 km along the state’s western coast, from Kasaragod in the north to Thiruvananthapuram in the south, linking ports, industrial clusters, and urban centers that together anchor Keralam’s coastal freight economy. Trucks account for 44% of carbon dioxide emissions from road transport in India despite comprising only 3% of the on-road fleet, and scaling up battery electric trucks (BETs) is central to India’s goal to reach net-zero emissions by 2070. Preparing a corridor like NH-66 for BETs requires knowing the number, type, location, and cost of the chargers needed. This corridor-level assessment has been absent for India’s freight routes. This report by the International Council on Clean Transportation, in partnership with Kerala State Electricity Board Limited, assesses the public electric vehicle charging infrastructure needed to support BET adoption along the corridor. Using FASTag toll data, national BET deployment projections, GPS-based truck parking data from 13,355 unique trucks and 339,692 parking events, and vehicle activity assumptions, the study quantifies charger counts, installed capacity, grid energy demand, and investment requirements through 2050, while identifying priority locations for charging infrastructure deployment. Key findings - Charging scale-up: NH-66 will need 1,939 chargers and 204.5 MW of installed capacity by 2050, up from just 90 chargers and 12.5 MW in 2030, as BET penetration rises across all truck segments. The corridor alone accounts for 78% of the total installed charger capacity projected across Keralam’s national highways. - Manageable grid impact: Charging demand will rise more than 26-fold by 2050, driven mainly by growing BET stock rather than fleet growth, but will remain below 0.2% of Keralam’s electricity consumption through 2040, indicating that state-level grid stress should stay manageable even as corridor demand accelerates. - Rising investment, within reach of current funding: Charging infrastructure investment is estimated at ₹19 crore by 2030 and ₹338 crore by 2050, with the pace accelerating sharply after 2030 as the number of chargers grows nearly eightfold between 2031 and 2040. The near-term requirement fits comfortably within approved PM E-DRIVE funding, though the estimates cover equipment costs only and exclude upstream grid upgrades. - Three charging hotspots: Kochi, Kozhikode, and Kollam emerge as priority locations based on GPS data from 13,355 trucks and 339,692 parking events. The Thiruvangad–Kumbalam section, the corridor’s longest and busiest, alone will require 76.4 MW by 2050, followed by Thalappady–Thiruvangad at 70.7 MW and Kumbalam–Thiruvallam at 57.4 MW.

title: Employment implications of vehicle electrification under alternative fuel efficiency pathways in India - International Council on Clean Transportation
source_name: 国际清洁交通委员会 ICCT
content: Report Employment implications of vehicle electrification under alternative fuel efficiency pathways in India Overview India’s automotive sector is a cornerstone of the national economy, contributing approximately 7.1% of national gross domestic product (GDP) and supporting nearly 30 million direct and indirect jobs. This report provides an economy-wide assessment of the industrial and labor market implications associated with the industry transition from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs). Specifically, it estimates the direct and indirect employment impacts of electrification under corporate average fuel efficiency (CAFE) norms of varying stringency levels. Using a demand-driven input–output (IO) framework based on an updated 2024 World Input-Output Database (WIOD) dataset for India, we developed a “synthetic” EV sector to explicitly model the distinct production structure of electric vehicles. We used three scenarios to assess the pace of India’s vehicle electrification transition through 2040. The Business as Usual (BAU) scenario reflects currently notified fuel efficiency regulations (CAFE II) and recent market trends, under which battery electric vehicles (BEVs) are projected to account for approximately 30% of new vehicle sales by 2040. The Industry Commitment scenario is based on announced automaker electrification targets, which would result in 100% BEV sales for passenger cars and two-wheelers by 2040. Finally, the Aligned with Viksit Bharat scenario represents a high-ambition pathway consistent with India’s long-term decarbonization and industrial development goals, achieving near-complete electrification across most vehicle segments by 2040. Under these scenarios, annual EV-related economic output is projected to increase from US$12.8 billion in 2024 to US$172.1 billion under the BAU scenario, US$506.1 billion under the Industry Commitment scenario, and US$620.5 billion under the Aligned with Viksit Bharat scenario by 2040. The transition is also expected to generate substantial employment across the economy. Under the Aligned with Viksit Bharat pathway, direct employment in core EV manufacturing, including vehicle assembly and key component production, is projected to increase from approximately 90,000 jobs in 2024 to 4.3 million jobs by 2040 under the baseline assumption of negligible battery localization; this rises to more than 7 million jobs assuming full domestic battery manufacturing. Indirect employment in the wider supply chain, including logistics, trade, finance, and professional services, is expected to be even larger, reaching approximately 17.3 million jobs by 2040, resulting in total EV-related employment exceeding 20 million jobs. However, the net employment balance—defined as the number of EV-related jobs created minus the jobs that would be expected to be transferred from the ICE sector or that would be exposed to the transition, meaning workers would likely requiring reskilling and redeployment—remains negative in the absence of domestic battery manufacturing. Once battery localization exceeds 25%, the net employment is positive across all transition scenarios, highlighting the critical role of domestic battery manufacturing in maximizing the employment benefits of India’s EV transition (figure below). Key findings Looking ahead to 2040, this capacity would be sufficient to achieve approximately 77% battery localization under the BAU scenario, requiring no additional manufacturing capacity to meet the assessed 50% localization target. By contrast, higher electrification pathways would necessitate further investments in battery manufacturing, requiring an additional 87 GWh under the Industry Commitment scenario and 112 GWh under the Aligned with Viksit Bharat scenario. Continued investment in domestic battery manufacturing will therefore be critical to support ambitious EV adoption while maximizing economic value addition and employment benefits. Although the net job impact is positive beyond a certain level of battery localization, approximately 60% of ICE-related manufacturing jobs are projected to be exposed to the transition, particularly in engine and transmission production. This underscores the importance of upskilling for roles with high overlap, like body shop operations and sales, and reskilling for specialized roles in high-voltage diagnostics, battery management systems, power electronics, and software integration. Policy recommendations Based on our findings on the employment impacts of various electrification pathways, we offer tailored considerations for effective policy design and implementation, including: - Regulatory certainty. Establishing increasingly stringent energy efficiency standards (or EV mandates) across all vehicle segments would help provide long-term investment clarity. - Strategic localization. Targeting at least 30% battery localization by 2032 and 50% by 2040 would help ensure that the shift to EVs creates more jobs than it displaces, transforming India’s EV transition into a net employment opportunity. Immediate priorities include expediting the PLI ACC scheme and expanding support to the broader battery ecosystem (e.g., production of active materials, battery recycling, and research and development). - Just transition. Implementing coordinated workforce programs could support the redeployment of ICE workers and equip the new workforce with multidisciplinary technical competencies.

title: India’s EV transition: Impact of electric vehicle battery demand on import payments from 2024 to 2050 - International Council on Clean Transportation
source_name: 国际清洁交通委员会 ICCT
content: Working Paper India’s EV transition: Impact of electric vehicle battery demand on import payments from 2024 to 2050 India’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales have grown rapidly, with a compound annual growth rate of 62.5% from fiscal year (FY) 2019–20 to FY 2024–25. Yet this growth has not been matched by growth in domestic battery manufacturing and India’s battery cell demand is currently met almost entirely through imports. As BEV adoption accelerates further, battery imports may continue to grow if local battery manufacturing supply chains remain inadequate, even as reliance on imported petrol and diesel declines. This study models India’s battery demand across all major on-road vehicle segments, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, buses, and trucks, from 2024 to 2050 under three BEV uptake scenarios. It then assesses how different levels of domestic battery manufacturing pathways could affect India’s combined oil and battery import payments. Faster electrification reduces India’s import payments even if batteries continue to be imported. Under the study’s reference oil-price assumptions, India’s combined oil and battery import bill in 2050 is 61% lower in the Ambitious electrification scenario than in the Baseline scenario, even with no domestic battery manufacturing. Across the study’s least and most favorable cases, the difference in India’s 2050 import bill reaches US$125 billion. Of that amount, US$94 billion is attributable to faster vehicle electrification, while an additional US$31 billion comes from greater domestic battery manufacturing. Avoided oil imports outweigh the cost of additional battery imports by an order of magnitude, making electrification the larger driver of import savings. Key takeaways - Battery demand grows substantially as vehicle electrification increases. Annual battery demand reaches about 340 GWh in the Baseline scenario and 573 GWh in both the Momentum and Ambitious scenarios by 2050. Faster electrification brings much of that demand forward, particularly before 2040. - Battery imports remain important in the near term. Domestic battery cell manufacturing is still at an early stage, meaning imports continue to play a significant role as battery demand grows. The different manufacturing pathways begin to diverge more substantially after 2030, with greater localization reducing battery import requirements over time. - Electrification has the largest impact on India’s future import payments. Even with no domestic battery manufacturing, the combined oil and battery import bill in 2050 is about 39% lower under the Momentum scenario and 61% lower under the Ambitious scenario than under the Baseline scenario. This is because the reduction in oil imports substantially outweighs the additional cost of battery imports. - Domestic battery manufacturing provides additional savings. Across the least and most favorable cases modeled, India’s 2050 import bill differs by US$125 billion. About three-quarters of that difference, US$94 billion, comes from faster electrification, while US$31 billion comes from scaling domestic battery manufacturing.
